opus-5.5.text:
I think a lot of it comes from where they started. Before DeepSeek, the team behind it came out of High-Flyer, a quantitative trading firm. In quant trading, every microsecond and every GPU dollar matters. You're running huge clusters and squeezing performance out of the hardware is a core skill. So they carried that mindset into large models: they weren't just training a model and handing it to someone else to serve. They thought about efficiency end to end.

You can see this in their model design. Multi-head latent attention, MLA, isn't just an accuracy trick. It's fundamentally about shrinking the KV cache so inference is cheaper and you can serve longer contexts with more concurrency. The fine-grained MoE with many small experts, the multi-token prediction for speculative decoding: these are architecture decisions made by people who are thinking, "How will this actually run on a GPU at serving time?" Most labs separate the modeling people from the systems people. DeepSeek seems to have them sitting together, or even the same people doing both.

The other part is constraint. They didn't have unlimited access to the newest hardware, so they had to go very low-level. They wrote their own kernels and dug into communication between GPUs. Then they open-sourced a lot of it during their open source week: FlashMLA, DeepEP for expert-parallel communication, DeepGEMM for FP8 matrix multiplication. Those aren't things you write unless you deeply understand the hardware down to the PTX level.

And the economics forced them to care. If you offer an API at a very low price and you have a huge number of users, inference cost is your survival. Training is a one-time cost, but inference is every single day. So they optimized large-scale deployment with things like prefill-decode disaggregation and large expert parallelism across many nodes, and they shared their numbers on throughput and cost margins. That level of transparency showed they had really engineered the whole serving system, not just the model.

So in short: a quant-trading engineering culture, co-design of model and system from day one, hardware constraints that pushed them down to the metal, and a business model where cheap inference was essential. Put those together and you get very deep inference expertise.

r001.rationale: The response links DeepSeek’s expertise to its origins at High-Flyer, a quantitative trading firm, and describes the team’s focus there on squeezing performance from hardware. This conveys the criterion’s earlier aggressive optimization work at the quant firm.

fable-5.1.text:
I think a lot of it traces back to the fact that DeepSeek, unlike most labs, has always treated inference as a first-class engineering problem rather than something you hand off after training is done. They came out of High-Flyer, which was a quant fund, and quant people live and die by latency and throughput. When your whole business is squeezing out efficiency on hardware, that mindset carries over. So from day one they were thinking about how a model actually runs, not just how it trains.

The second piece is that they build their own infrastructure end to end. They don't just rent cloud GPUs and call an API. They wrote their own kernels, their own communication libraries, their own scheduling. When you own the full stack, you see where the real bottlenecks are, and you're forced to understand things at a depth that most teams never reach. That's where ideas like MLA and the way they handle MoE routing at serving time come from. Those aren't things you invent by reading papers. You invent them by staring at profiler traces and asking why the GPU is idle.

And third, honestly, they were constrained. They couldn't get the newest hardware in unlimited quantities, so they had to make older or fewer chips do more work. Constraint is a great teacher. If you have infinite compute, you never learn to be clever. They had to be clever, and they open-sourced a lot of it, which is why the whole community, including vLLM, has learned from what they did.

r001.rationale: The response links DeepSeek’s inference expertise to its origins at High-Flyer, a quant fund, where latency, throughput, and hardware efficiency were central concerns.

astra-6.text:
My guess is that it comes from working closely across models and systems. When you train and serve your own models, you get direct feedback on where inference is expensive, and you can make changes on both sides: how the model is designed and how it runs on the hardware. Over time, those decisions build on one another.

I don’t have inside knowledge of DeepSeek’s team, so I wouldn’t attribute it to one particular person or technique. I’d think of it as accumulated expertise from repeatedly solving those problems.

r001.rationale: The response attributes the expertise to accumulated experience optimizing models and systems, but does not mention earlier aggressive performance optimization work at Huanfang Quantization.

sol-6.1.text:
My guess is that it comes from working on training and inference together. When you design the model yourself, you understand which parts are expensive and where you can make tradeoffs. Then inference becomes part of the model design, rather than something you optimize only after training is finished.

But I don’t know their internal history, so I’d be cautious about attributing that expertise to any particular person or project.

r001.rationale: The candidate attributes the expertise to designing and optimizing training and inference together, and explicitly avoids naming any particular prior project. It does not mention Huanfang Quantization or its aggressive performance optimization work.
